Looking at the first option: "ز بس کردم شمار جرم خود فرسوده شددستم - کسی تا کی حساب ریگ صحرا را نگه دارد؟" The words "جرم" (crime, sin), "فرسوده شددستم" (my hands have become worn out), and "حساب ریگ صحرا" (counting the sins of the desert) stand out. It seems to be about the speaker's own sins and the burden of counting them, maybe questioning who can hold onto that count.

Second option: "ریگ صحرا را بر جرم من افزونی نیست - لیک بخشایش او راست به جرمم بیشی" Here, "ریگ صحرا" (desert sin) is mentioned again, but this time it's saying that the desert sin isn't added to my crime, but if he forgives, then my crime is more. This might be about the speaker's guilt or the idea that their own sins are greater than others'.

Third option: "چشم گشا و رو نگر جُ رم بیار و خو نگر - خوی چو آبِ جو نگر جمله طراوت و صفا" The words "چشم گشا" (open your eyes), "رو نگر" (look at the face), "خو نگر" (look at the self), and "آبِ جو نگر" (water of the gaze) are here. This seems more metaphorical, maybe about self-reflection or seeing the truth, with "خوی" possibly referring to the soul or inner self. The mention of "طرافت و صفا" (freshness and purity) suggests a theme of clarity or purity.

Fourth option: "پیشانی عفو تو را پرچین نسازد جرم ما - آیینه کی بر هم خورد از زشتی تمثال ها" "پیشانی عفو تو" (the forehead of your forgiveness) and "آیینه" (mirror) are key. It might be saying that our sins shouldn't tarnish your forgiveness, and the mirror is shattered by the ugliness of statues. This could relate to the impact of sins on divine forgiveness and the destruction of beauty by ugliness.

Now, comparing all four. The first three options (1, 2, 4) all mention "ریگ صحرا" (desert sin) or similar terms, and they deal with themes of sin, guilt, and forgiveness. The third option (3) doesn't mention "ریگ صحرا" and instead talks about opening eyes, looking at the self, and purity. The focus here seems more on self-awareness or introspection rather than sin and forgiveness. So option 3 is the outlier.
